newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Key Gazprom decisions May 16 - Chubais.
newsitem.headline: Key Gazprom decisions May 16 - Chubais.

text.p: Key decisions on restructuring Russian natural gas giant Gazprom will be taken by government officials at a meeting with the company on May 16, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais was quoted as saying.
Interfax news agency said Chubais, the government's economic supremo, made the remarks before setting off on Saturday for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) meeting in Washington.

Gazprom, the world's biggest gas producer and a powerful player in Russia's attempts to create a market economy, has prepared a restructuring plan that includes shedding 100,000 jobs or 26 percent of its workforce.

Chubais said the government committee which would meet on May 16 was examining the firm's proposals and principal decisions would be taken on tariff policy, price differentials and the "openness" of Gazprom and the market in its shares.

The head of Gazprom -- whose predecessor, Viktor Chernomyrdin, is now prime minister -- has said the company has settled differences with the government and asserted that the company will remain a monopoly and will not be split up.

Gazprom has come under attack by the IMF and some government officials over its opaque finances. The state has a 40 percent stake in Gazprom, seven-eighths of it personally managed in trust by the company's chairman.
Chubais, 41, denied any rift over policy on dealing with natural monopolies between Chernomyrdin and the young reformers brought into the cabinet by President Boris Yeltsin last month.

Natural monopoly is a standard economic expression used in Russia to describe businesses where, by their nature, competition is viewed as difficult and unusual -- such as household gas and electricity supplies, telephone networks and railways.
Yeltsin put Chubais's fellow first deputy premier, Boris Nemtsov, 37, in charge of the energy ministry last week.
Russia accounts for 34 percent of world gas reserves and 27 percent of output; Gazprom produces nearly all of Russia's gas. ((--Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520))
